arXiv:2609.13267v1 [cs.CV] 07 Sep 2026

Structure-Token Evidence-Anchored Reasoning for Scientific Chart Understanding

Alberlucia Rafael Soarez    Camila Ferreira    Daniel Kim    Mariana Costa    Alejandro Torres Affiliation: University of Brasilia Email: alejandro.torres@iscon.edu.br
Abstract

Scientific charts encode quantities in axes, legends, and geometric marks, yet large vision–language models still treat them as natural photographs. Visual in-context examples do not expose the coordinate frame; unconstrained chain-of-thought can name a plausible number that was never read from a bar. We present STEER (Structure-Token Evidence-anchored Reasoning), which freezes a Llama-3.2-Vision encoder and inserts three modules: a chart structure graph encoder (CSGE) that binds ticks, legend items, and marks; evidence-anchored step reasoning (EASR) that forces every arithmetic step to cite a graph node; and weak-parser strong-reasoner alignment (WPSR) that uses a specialized table extractor only as a teacher of node attributes. On ChartQA, STEER reaches 82.70 average relaxed accuracy versus 80.16 for ChartGemma and 76.40 for a LLaVA-CoT backbone trained on the same mix. Gains widen on CharXiv reasoning (33.60 vs. 29.20 InternVL Chat V1.5) and ChartQAPro CoT (40.70 vs. 37.17 Qwen2-VL-7B), where OCR shortcuts disappear. Ablations show that dropping node serialization or numeric candidate constraints undoes most of the reasoning lift.

1 Introduction

Charts are the default carrier of quantitative claims in papers, filings, and policy briefs. A model that can answer “which series peaked first?” or “what is the 2019–2021 ratio?” would unlock scientific search and financial monitoring, including settings where numerical claims sit beside noisy social-media timestamps (Hu and Shen, 2026). Progress on ChartQA looks strong: specialist models report average relaxed accuracy above 80 (Masry et al., 2025b; Masry et al., 2022). The same systems collapse once the chart is an arXiv figure (Wang et al., 2024b), an unannotated plot (Xu et al., 2023), or a dashboard from a previously unseen publisher (Masry et al., 2025a). The failure is not generic visual question answering. It is a mismatch between how charts are drawn and how current large vision–language models (LVLMs) are trained.

Three practices dominate. First, visual in-context learning concatenates whole-image exemplars and hopes the query chart will be read by analogy (Zhou et al., 2024). Similarity in layout is a weak proxy for a shared coordinate frame: two bar charts can look alike while their yy-axes differ by an order of magnitude. Second, free-form chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2025) writes a fluent rationale that need not point at a mark. ChartR shows that early extraction errors propagate through later arithmetic (Chen et al., 2026); ChartAgent recovers some of that gap only by calling external drawing tools (Kaur et al., 2026). Third, chart-specialist parsers (Liu et al., 2023; Masry et al., 2023) extract tables well inside ChartQA’s distribution and fail on ChartQAPro, where ChartGemma’s CoT overall is 9.80 (Masry et al., 2025a). A strong general LVLM and a weak specialist currently have no shared channel for node-level attributes.

We keep Llama-3.2-Vision with a LLaVA-CoT training recipe (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025) and insert three modules (Figure 1). CSGE builds a typed graph of axes, ticks, legend items, and marks, then mixes graph states into visual tokens. EASR replaces unconstrained stages with a loop that must emit an evidence address before a number. WPSR treats the specialist parser as a weak teacher of cells, not as the answerer, following the weak-to-strong transfer motif without copying its LLM-only protocol (Zhou et al., 2025a). Contributions:

  • •

    CSGE makes the coordinate frame an explicit graph rather than a hope of in-context copying.

  • •

    EASR binds every reasoning step to a node or box so numeric tokens can be filtered at decode time.

  • •

    WPSR aligns a strong reasoner to a weak parser on high-confidence cells and keeps 20% non-chart data so multi-capability behaviour does not collapse. STEER reaches 82.70 ChartQA avg, 33.60 CharXiv reasoning, 51.00 ChartBench Acc+, and 40.70 ChartQAPro CoT.

2 Related Work

2.1 Chart understanding models and benchmarks

Early ChartQA systems assumed a recovered table and ran TaPas or T5 on flattened cells (Masry et al., 2022). Pix2Struct, MatCha, and UniChart moved the stack onto screenshot parsing and chart-to-table pretraining (Lee et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Masry et al., 2023). Instruction-tuned chart LVLMs—ChartLlama, ChartInstruct, ChartAssistant, ChartGemma, TinyChart—raise ChartQA averages into the 60–80 range (Han et al., 2023; Masry et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2024; Masry et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2024). They still flatten the image: the axis is a pixel pattern, not a typed node. CharXiv splits descriptive and reasoning questions on 2,323 arXiv figures and finds a 33.4 point gap from GPT-4o (47.10) to humans (80.50) on reasoning (Wang et al., 2024b; OpenAI, 2024). ChartBench stresses unannotated marks with Acc+ (Xu et al., 2023); ChartQAPro adds dashboards, infographics, dialogue, and unanswerable items (Masry et al., 2025a). 2026 evaluations push further: ChartR decomposes multi-step traces (Chen et al., 2026), LongChart targets multi-image sets (Xiao et al., 2026), and ChartQA-X asks for faithful explanations rather than a number alone (Hegde et al., 2026). Retrieval-augmented VQA shows that looking up an external passage is not a substitute for reading the figure (Lin and Byrne, 2022; Chen et al., 2023).

2.2 Visual reasoning, graphs, and localized feedback

LLaVA-style instruction tuning made general LVLMs usable on charts without a table (Liu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2024b; Chen et al., 2024a). Structured CoT with stage tags improves MMStar and MathVista (Xu et al., 2025); Visual CoT predicts boxes for natural objects (Shao et al., 2024). IdealGPT decomposes vision–language questions iteratively (You et al., 2023). Chart-FR1 links steps to local crops on dense charts (Pan et al., 2026); ChartAgent edits the pixels with tools (Kaur et al., 2026). None of these methods compile a legend–mark graph. Multimodal graph transformers and knowledge-graph QA already treat entities as nodes (He and Wang, 2023; Hu et al., 2022; Perez-Beltrachini et al., 2023). CSGE reuses that inductive bias for axes and marks. Localized supervision is closest to abnormal-aware medical feedback, which backpropagates through lesion regions rather than whole images (Zhou et al., 2025b); we relocate the idea from pathology to ticks. Physics-coherent generation work aligns 2D features with 3D structure (Xiong et al., 2026a)—a reminder that geometry-aware alignment helps when pixels alone are under-determined.

2.3 Alignment, faithfulness, and sample selection

Weak-to-strong generalization studies how a weaker supervisor can lift a stronger student across several skills (Zhou et al., 2025a). Contextual faithfulness can be taught with synthetic tasks and reinforcement (Si et al., 2026a). GATEAU selects influential long-context samples before alignment (Si et al., 2025). We do not rerun those LLM-only protocols. WPSR uses a chart parser as the weak supervisor of cells, keeps the strong model as the answerer, and mixes non-chart LLaVA-CoT data so the student does not overfit tables. Interactive world models store action-aware memory (Xiong et al., 2026b); our memory is a static structure graph, not an explorable environment.

3 Method

A chart image II and question qq map to an answer yy as in equation 1. Figure 1 shows the flow. The vision backbone follows Llama-3.2-Vision (Grattafiori et al., 2024); LoRA adapters sit on the language model (Hu et al., 2021). CSGE, EASR, and WPSR are the trainable additions.

3.1 Problem and visual tokens

Let V=Enc⁡(I)∈ℝP×dV=\mathrm{Enc}(I)\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times d} be patch tokens. The decoder produces yy under a constraint that numeric spans come from a candidate set built by EASR:

y\displaystyle y =fθ​(I,q)=Dec⁡([V′;q],𝒞⁡(G)),\displaystyle=f_{\theta}(I,q)=\mathrm{Dec}([V^{\prime};\,q],\,\mathcal{C}(G)), (1)

where V′V^{\prime} is the structure-mixed sequence in equation 6 and 𝒞⁡(G)\mathcal{C}(G) is the numeric candidate table. Encoding is

V\displaystyle V =Enc⁡(I),Q=Tok⁡(q).\displaystyle=\mathrm{Enc}(I),\qquad Q=\mathrm{Tok}(q). (2)

Without CSGE, VV in equation 2 is a natural-image embedding. Charts violate that assumption: the same ink length can mean 3 or 30 depending on the axis.

3.2 CSGE: chart structure graph encoder

A DETR-style head (Carion et al., 2020) predicts a set of primitives with types in {x​-​axis,y​-​axis,tick,legend,bar,line,slice,text}\{\mathrm{x\text{-}axis},\mathrm{y\text{-}axis},\mathrm{tick},\mathrm{legend},\mathrm{bar},\mathrm{line},\mathrm{slice},\mathrm{text}\}. Node ii carries type, box, OCR string, and a colour histogram cic_{i}:

ni\displaystyle n_{i} =[etype​(ti);MLP⁡(bi);eocr​(si);ci].\displaystyle=[\,e_{\mathrm{type}}(t_{i});\;\mathrm{MLP}(b_{i});\;e_{\mathrm{ocr}}(s_{i});\;c_{i}\,]. (3)

The concatenation in equation 3 is the structure token. Legend–mark edges use colour and relative position,

wi​j\displaystyle w_{ij} =σ⁡(cos⁡(ci,cj)+α​rel​(bi,bj)),\displaystyle=\sigma\!\left(\cos(c_{i},c_{j})+\alpha\,\mathrm{rel}(b_{i},b_{j})\right), (4)

and we keep the edge if wi​jw_{ij} in equation 4 exceeds 0.6. Axis–tick and tick–mark edges are geometric (projection onto the nearest axis). Two R-GCN layers (Schlichtkrull et al., 2018) update nodes:

hi(ℓ+1)\displaystyle h_{i}^{(\ell+1)} =ReLU⁡(W0​hi(ℓ)+∑r,j∈𝒩r​(i)1|𝒩r​(i)|​Wr​hj(ℓ)).\displaystyle=\mathrm{ReLU}\!\Big(W_{0}h_{i}^{(\ell)}+\sum_{r,j\in\mathcal{N}_{r}(i)}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}_{r}(i)|}W_{r}h_{j}^{(\ell)}\Big). (5)

Let G=[h1,…,h|N|]G=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{|N|}] after equation 5. Visual tokens attend to GG,

V′\displaystyle V^{\prime} =V+softmax⁡((V​Wq)​(G​Wk)⊤d)​G​Wv.\displaystyle=V+\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{(VW_{q})(GW_{k})^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)GW_{v}. (6)

The LLM also receives a serialized node table (id,ti,si)(\mathrm{id},t_{i},s_{i}). Removing that table in ablation drops ChartQA avg from 82.70 to 80.35, so the language side must see the graph, not only the pixels in equation 6.

3.3 EASR: evidence-anchored step reasoning

LLaVA-CoT uses four unconstrained stages (Xu et al., 2025). EASR instead runs K=6K{=}6 steps (default). At step kk the model predicts an address aka_{k} over nodes and optional boxes:

p⁡(ak∣a<k,q,V′)\displaystyle p(a_{k}\mid a_{<k},q,V^{\prime}) =softmax⁡(u⊤​tanh⁡(W⁡[ha;v¯;Q])).\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}(u^{\top}\tanh(W[h_{a};\,\bar{v};\,Q])). (7)

Equation equation 7 is a pointer, not free text. A readout copies attributes from the chosen node,

rk\displaystyle r_{k} =Read⁡(G,ak,V′)=[sak;v^ak;crop⁡(I,bak)],\displaystyle=\mathrm{Read}(G,a_{k},V^{\prime})=[s_{a_{k}};\;\hat{v}_{a_{k}};\;\mathrm{crop}(I,b_{a_{k}})], (8)

where v^\hat{v} in equation 8 is a value head trained on SVG boxes from ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022). An aggregation head implements {sum,diff,ratio,argmax,lookup}\{\mathrm{sum},\mathrm{diff},\mathrm{ratio},\mathrm{argmax},\mathrm{lookup}\}:

y^\displaystyle\hat{y} =Agg(r1:K,op).\displaystyle=\mathrm{Agg}(r_{1:K},\;\mathrm{op}). (9)

The step text sks_{k} is trained with teacher forcing,

ℒstep\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{step}} =−∑k=1Klogp(sk,ak∣s<k,q,V′),\displaystyle=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\log p(s_{k},a_{k}\mid s_{<k},q,V^{\prime}), (10)

and decoding rejects a numeric span that is not in {v^ak}∪{y^}\{\hat{v}_{a_{k}}\}\cup\{\hat{y}\} from equation 9:

Reject⁡(y)\displaystyle\mathrm{Reject}(y) =[num(y)∉𝒞(G)].\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\mathrm{num}(y)\notin\mathcal{C}(G)\right]. (11)

Equation equation 11 is the chart analogue of faithfulness filters trained with synthetic tasks (Si et al., 2026a): the generator may not invent a year that no tick contains. Medical abnormal-aware training localizes a lesion (Zhou et al., 2025b); EASR localizes a mark. Focus-CoT also cites crops (Pan et al., 2026), but it does not compile a legend graph, so colour aliases remain unbound.

3.4 WPSR: weak-parser strong-reasoner alignment

Let PwP_{w} be a frozen MatCha/UniChart-style extractor (Liu et al., 2023; Masry et al., 2023) that emits a table TwT_{w} with cell-wise confidence. The student emits TsT_{s} from CSGE nodes. Alignment is ℓ1\ell_{1} on cells with confidence above 0.8:

ℒalign\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}} =∑u,v𝟏[cu​v>0.8]∥Ts[u,v]−Tw[u,v]∥1.\displaystyle=\sum_{u,v}\mathbf{1}[c_{uv}>0.8]\,\lVert T_{s}[u,v]-T_{w}[u,v]\rVert_{1}. (12)

The answer loss is standard token CE,

ℒans\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ans}} =−log⁡pθ​(y∣I,q).\displaystyle=-\log p_{\theta}(y\mid I,q). (13)

EASR adds the step loss from equation 10,

ℒeasr\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{easr}} =ℒstep+β​𝔼​[Reject⁡(y)].\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{step}}+\beta\,\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Reject}(y)]. (14)

Equation equation 12 never trains PwP_{w} to emit yy; equation 13 remains the only answer CE. Equation equation 14 adds the reject penalty. The total objective is

ℒ\displaystyle\mathcal{L} =ℒans+λ​ℒalign+μ​ℒeasr,\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ans}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}+\mu\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{easr}}, (15)

with λ=0.3\lambda{=}0.3, μ=1\mu{=}1, β=0.2\beta{=}0.2. This is weak-to-strong transfer for chart cells (Zhou et al., 2025a): PwP_{w} never answers at test time, which avoids the ChartQAPro collapse of specialists. Twenty percent of each batch is non-chart LLaVA-CoT-100k so general VQA does not vanish.

3.5 Training schedule and complexity

Stage 1 trains the CSGE detector on ChartQA SVG boxes and synthetic charts for two epochs with Enc frozen. Stage 2 opens WPSR with λ=0.3\lambda{=}0.3 for two epochs. Stage 3 jointly LoRA-tunes the LLM and EASR for three epochs on ChartQA train plus ChartBench train. Inference disables PwP_{w}. Let PP be patches, NN nodes (N≪PN\ll P), KK steps. Extra cost over the backbone is

𝒪⁡(P​N+N2+K​d2),\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(PN+N^{2}+K\,d^{2}), (16)

dominated by the KK decode passes in equation 16, matching the latency table in Section 6.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Datasets and protocol

Table 1 lists the four evaluation sets. ChartQA reports relaxed accuracy on human (H) and machine (M) questions (Masry et al., 2022). We follow the modern VLM protocol of ChartGemma (aug. / human / avg) for the main table (Masry et al., 2025b) and keep the 2022 table-QA numbers only as historical context. CharXiv uses the official validation split of 1,000 charts (Wang et al., 2024b). ChartBench reports Acc+ averaged over regular and extra types (Xu et al., 2023); its ChartQA column in the original paper is zero-shot and is not mixed with our fine-tuned ChartQA numbers. ChartQAPro uses the authors’ Direct / CoT / PoT prompts; CoT is our default (Masry et al., 2025a). Relaxed accuracy allows a 5% relative error on numeric answers,

RA⁡(y,y^)\displaystyle\mathrm{RA}(y,\hat{y}) =[|y−y^|max⁡(|y|,10−8)≤0.05].\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\frac{|y-\hat{y}|}{\max(|y|,10^{-8})}\leq 0.05\right]. (17)

ChartQAPro additionally uses ANLS for text and exact match for years (Masry et al., 2025a). We report equation 17 on ChartQA, CharXiv numeric items, and ChartQAPro numeric items.

4.2 Baselines and implementation

Open-source chart specialists: Pix2Struct, MatCha, UniChart, ChartLlama, ChartInstruct, ChartAssistant, ChartGemma, TinyChart (Lee et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Masry et al., 2023; Han et al., 2023; Masry et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2024; Masry et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2024). General LVLMs: LLaVA-1.5/1.6, Qwen2-VL, InternVL Chat V1.5 / InternVL2.5, Llama-3.2-Vision, MiniCPM-V, DocOwl-1.5, InternLM-XComposer2 (Liu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2024a; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2024). Visual reasoning: LLaVA-CoT and Visual CoT (Xu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024). Closed models (GPT-4o/V, Claude, Gemini) are reference rows only (OpenAI, 2024; OpenAI, 2023; Anthropic, 2024; Team et al., 2023). Our backbone is Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct with LoRA rank 64, α=128\alpha{=}128, trained on 8×\timesA100 80GB. Unless noted, STEER (CSGE+EASR+WPSR) is the full model.

5 Results

5.1 ChartQA

Table 2 reports the modern protocol. ChartGemma reaches 80.16 avg (Masry et al., 2025b). A LLaVA-CoT model fine-tuned on the ChartQA training split reaches 76.40. STEER reaches 82.70 (+2.54 vs. ChartGemma, +6.30 vs. the backbone). The human split moves from 69.52 to 73.24; the synthetic aug. split (92.16) stays below ChartAssistant’s 93.90 (Meng et al., 2024). That pattern is intended: CSGE and EASR target compositional human questions, not template lookup. GPT-4V sits at 78.5 and is not in the open ranking (OpenAI, 2023).

Sensitivity, shift, and efficiency plots appear in Figures 2(a)–3(b); Section 6 interprets them.

5.2 CharXiv

Table 3 uses validation reasoning and descriptive accuracy (Wang et al., 2024b). InternVL Chat V1.5 is the strongest published open model at 29.20 / 58.50. LLaVA-CoT reaches 27.40 / 55.80. STEER reaches 33.60 / 61.90 (+4.40 / +3.40 vs. InternVL). GPT-4o remains far ahead at 47.10 / 84.45 (OpenAI, 2024). The larger relative gain on reasoning matches CSGE’s role: descriptive questions often need OCR, while reasoning questions need legend–mark binding across subplots.

5.3 ChartBench

Table 4 reports Acc+ Avg. InternLM-XComposer-v2 leads published open models at 47.78 (Dong et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2023). STEER reaches 51.00 (+3.22). Value extraction Acc+ moves from 36.63 to 41.80; that is the unannotated-mark case ChartBench was built to isolate. GPT-4o sits at 59.45 as a closed ceiling (OpenAI, 2024). We do not fill the paper’s zero-shot ChartQA column: that protocol is not our fine-tuned ChartQA setting.

5.4 ChartQAPro

Table 5 is the out-of-publisher stress test (Masry et al., 2025a). Specialists collapse (ChartGemma CoT 9.80, TinyChart 11.67). Qwen2-VL-7B is the strongest open CoT overall at 37.17 (Wang et al., 2024a); InternVL2.5-8B leads Direct at 35.67 (Chen et al., 2024a). Llama-3.2-Vision-11B scores 11.09 Direct because it ignores the prompt style (Grattafiori et al., 2024). LLaVA-CoT recovers to 29.80 CoT. STEER reaches 38.90 Direct and 40.70 CoT (+3.53 vs. Qwen2-VL CoT). Claude Sonnet 3.5 remains at 55.81 CoT (Anthropic, 2024). Phi-3.5-Vision and Ovis are listed for completeness as published open systems on this split (Abdin et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024). ChartQA-X style explanations are complementary: we constrain numbers, they score free text (Hegde et al., 2026).

5.5 Ablation

Table 6 uses one backbone, one mix, and one seed family. Each single module beats LLaVA-CoT. CSGE+EASR already reaches 81.15 ChartQA avg; WPSR adds the last 1.55 by cleaning cell attributes. The three single-module ChartQA gains sum to 6.65 versus a full gain of 6.30, so the modules overlap on nodes. Removing node serialization or the numeric filter of equation 11 costs 2.35 and 1.30 avg respectively: the graph must enter the prompt, and the decoder must not freely sample years.

6 Analysis

Hyperparameters.

Figure 2 (left) and Figure 2(a) sweep EASR’s step cap KK. ChartQA avg peaks at K=6K{=}6 (82.70) and falls to 81.70 at K=10K{=}10 as empty evidence steps inject noise, while latency grows almost linearly. The alignment weight λ\lambda in equation 15 peaks at 0.3; λ=0\lambda{=}0 recovers CSGE+EASR (81.15) and λ=1.0\lambda{=}1.0 overfits TwT_{w} (80.40). Two R-GCN layers beat one (81.60) and four (81.95).

Shift.

Figure 2(b) plots LLaVA-CoT versus STEER across domains. In-domain ChartQA Δ\Delta is +6.30 vs. the backbone but only +2.54 vs. ChartGemma. ChartBench without point labels, CharXiv reasoning, and ChartQAPro are the harder shifts; Δ\Delta vs. the backbone stays in +6.20+6.20 to +10.90+10.90, while Δ\Delta vs. the best published open model stays inside +3.2+3.2 to +4.4+4.4. Table 7 splits ChartQAPro by visual family: dashboards give the largest gap versus Qwen2-VL-7B (+6.29), consistent with CSGE’s subplot axes.

Efficiency.

Figure 3 collects the radar and Pareto views. Figure 3(a) summarizes relative gains; Figure 3(b) places variants on the accuracy–latency plane. CSGE adds 150 ms, EASR 320 ms, WPSR almost nothing at test time. Full latency is 1385 ms/image on A100 versus 890 ms for LLaVA-CoT and 420 ms for ChartGemma-3B. The 3B specialist is faster and close on ChartQA, and unusable on ChartQAPro. Interactive memories in world models amortize cost across actions (Xiong et al., 2026b); we pay the graph cost once per static figure.

Failures.

On 100 CharXiv reasoning errors, 42 bind the wrong subplot axis, 27 treat a log or dual axis as linear, 18 confuse texture legends with colour, and 13 need the caption paragraph. On ChartQAPro unanswerable items STEER Direct is 44.20 versus 53.92 for InternVL2.5-8B (Chen et al., 2024a; Masry et al., 2025a): evidence constraints still prefer to read the nearest bar rather than abstain. LongChart-style multi-figure inputs are out of scope (Xiao et al., 2026).

7 Conclusion

Charts are structure plus ink. STEER makes that structure a graph, insists that each arithmetic step name a node, and uses a weak parser only as a teacher of cells. The design is deliberately not visual in-context learning (Zhou et al., 2024), not medical lesion feedback (Zhou et al., 2025b), and not a tool-using agent (Kaur et al., 2026). It improves open LVLMs on ChartQA, CharXiv, ChartBench, and ChartQAPro without overtaking closed GPT-4o. A global planner for long-horizon agents remains future work: EASR’s step loop is local, not a goal-conditioned plan over many figures (Si et al., 2026b). We also need an explicit abstention head and better dual-axis parsers. Code and graphs will follow the paper.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
